items.title: An Interactive Assistant to Support Security Operators
items.abstract: The security of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) is paramount, yet human operators frequently face cognitive overload when managing complex cyber-physical threats. This chapter presents a comprehensive overview of AVATAR4BC, a novel, personalized Intelligent Virtual Assistant (IVA) designed to address this critical human-factors challenge. Our system represents a paradigm shift from traditional dashboards by providing an embodied, conversational interface that leverages a high-fidelity 3D human avatar. A core contribution of AVATAR4BC is its multidisciplinary approach, which goes beyond technical integration. It fuses advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) with insights from the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH). The system’s backend integrates Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), and real-time speech-driven facial animation to create a natural interaction. Crucially, it incorporates Explainable AI (XAI) principles by using Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate human-readable explanations of opaque Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent decisions from the underlying DYNABIC framework. Furthermore, AVATAR4BC’s personalization engine, informed by psychological and behavioral research, dynamically adapts the avatar’s appearance, voice, and communication style to the operator, aiming to reduce stress and enhance decision-making effectiveness. Final validation through end-to-end unit testing demonstrates the system’s core functionality, confirming the seamless integration of its architectural components. This work establishes a robust foundation for future research into human–AI collaboration, with significant implications for enhancing resilience in cybersecurity and other high-stakes domains.

items.title: Application and Optimization of Multimodal Knowledge Management in Web-Based English Teaching
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of digital transformation, English teaching is constrained by over-reliance on single-modal resources and insufficient integration of web technologies and pedagogy, which hinder the development of learners' higher-order skills. Using mixed-methods research, this study constructs a cognition-centered multimodal knowledge management framework based on cognitive load theory. It develops a system for resource classification, scenario adaptation, and cognitive activation alongside a three-dimensional tagging mechanism and an augmented reality‒supported technology-teaching double-helix model. Proper visual‒auditory input matching facilitates learners' information retention. Empirical evaluation reveals positive changes in classroom group interaction, digital tool adoption, and students' written logical performance. This study offers practical optimization strategies and suggests bridging the digital divide, strengthening teachers' technological pedagogical content knowledge capability, and exploring artificial intelligence applications for web-based multimodal English teaching.

items.title: APPLICATION OF DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES IN THE USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
items.abstract: This article analyzes the possibilities of applying modern digital technologies in solar energy systems. It examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), the Internet of Things (IoT), Digital Twin, Edge AI, cloud computing, Big Data, blockchain, drones, robotic maintenance, GIS, SCADA, smart inverters, and AR/VR technologies to improve the efficiency of solar photovoltaic power plants, forecast electricity generation, detect technical faults at an early stage, and optimize energy flow management. Digital technologies make it possible to monitor the real-time status of solar energy facilities, forecast power generation based on meteorological data, detect faults in panels and inverters, and automate maintenance. The article also highlights promising directions, including AI-based Digital Twins, Edge AI, federated learning, autonomous drone inspection, and blockchain-based peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading.

items.title: Applications of Geographic Information Systems in Natural-Resource Management: A Critical Review of Methods, Evidence, Validation and Future Directions
items.abstract: Natural-resource management (NRM) increasingly depends on spatially explicit evidence because land, soil, water, forests and vegetation vary across space and change through time. Geographic Information Systems (GIS), often integrated with remote sensing (RS), provide a common analytical environment for resource inventory, multi-layer integration, change detection, suitability assessment and decision support. This review synthesises a curated corpus of 20 records representing 19 unique studies published between 1995 and 2026; one duplicated Kumar, Yamaç and Velmurugan record was removed before synthesis. The evidence was organised into six domains: (i) planning, decision support and participatory GIS; (ii) multi-sector RS–GIS applications; (iii) soil resources and land degradation; (iv) land-use/land-cover (LULC) change, forests and watershed programmes; (v) water and groundwater; and (vi) agriculture, climate and crop modelling. Across the corpus, overlay analysis, terrain analysis and multi-temporal change detection are the most recurrent GIS functions. Empirical evidence is strongly concentrated in Indian watershed studies. Reported LULC classification accuracies in three case-study groups range from 89.70% to approximately 95%, although these values are not directly comparable because imagery, class schemes and validation designs differ. The synthesis identifies persistent weaknesses in data quality and spatial resolution, field validation, uncertainty reporting, generalisability, subjective weighting in multi-criteria decision-making, limited temporal density, and unequal technical access. Fifteen of the 19 studies explicitly point towards artificial intelligence or machine learning as an emerging opportunity, while UAV/LiDAR data, IoT observations, cloud processing, predictive modelling and participatory web/mobile GIS remain underused. We argue that the next generation of GIS-based NRM should move from static and retrospective mapping towards dynamic, field-validated, uncertainty-aware, predictive and participatory decision systems. A validation-centred framework and a prioritised research agenda are proposed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Acceptance Among Nurses and Other Healthcare Professionals in Spain and Henan Province, China: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Comparison
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Assessing artificial intelligence (AI) acceptance may help identify questions for nursing education, but similar overall scores need not reflect similar response patterns. We compared general AI acceptance in healthcare professional samples from Spain and Henan Province, China, including a substantial nursing subgroup. Methods: This exploratory cross-sectional comparison used data from two convenience-sampled online surveys involving 7187 respondents (Spain, 3764; Henan, 3423), including 3590 nurses. We examined a five-item acceptance composite using ordinal confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance testing, observed and adjusted comparisons, and equivalence testing with bounds of ±0.20 pooled standard deviations. Results: Observed means were 3.59 in Spain and 3.56 in Henan; the difference of 0.028 points fell within the exploratory equivalence bounds (90% CI −0.010 to 0.067; bounds ±0.195), whose practical significance has not been established. Metric and scalar constraints met change-in-fit criteria, although absolute fit was mixed and strict invariance was not supported. The scalar model yielded an exploratory latent Henan–Spain contrast of 0.227 reference-group standard deviations (95% CI 0.152 to 0.302), which requires caution given the mixed model fit. The adjusted composite difference was 0.114 points (95% CI 0.054 to 0.173). Item-level differences ran in opposing directions. In the exploratory nursing subgroup analysis, the adjusted Henan–Spain difference was 0.081 points (95% CI −0.014 to 0.176; Holm-adjusted p = 0.283). The interval included zero and positive differences; nurse-specific equivalence was not tested. Conclusions: Similar observed averages concealed heterogeneous responses in these samples. The findings support examining distinct aspects of acceptance when designing nursing-focused needs assessments, not assuming competence or readiness for a particular AI tool. Non-probability recruitment and incomplete cross-cultural validation limit generalization and interpretation. Registration: The study was not registered.

items.abstract: The fast development of artificial intelligence (AI) is essentially transforming the sphere of travel and tourism. In this chapter, the author provides an in-depth discussion of AI application in key sectors of personalization, customer service automation, revenue management, destination management, hospitality management, transportation and sustainability. According to the current studies and industry dynamics, the chapter is very useful in studying the development of technology in the tourism industry- starting with primitive Global Distribution Systems to the current machine learning systems. Nevertheless, the transformative potential of AI cannot be undervalued, and so is the ethical issue related to its implementation, including the privacy of data, replacing people with a machine, and the biases of the algorithm. Exploring and analyzing challenges, especially in the developing world.The chapter ends by presenting new trends which include generative AI and augmented reality and the metaverse as a research framework that scholars and practitioners can use to study.

items.title: Artificial intelligence applications in forensic science and their implications for education and training
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly relevant to forensic practice and has potential applications in forensic education, including evidence interpretation, simulation-based learning, and decision-making. Then, evidence regarding its educational implementation remains fragmented, with limited consensus on pedagogical frameworks and competency development. Methodology A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 were identified through Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Eligible studies for the primary synthesis were required to include an identifiable forensic educational or training context, an AI-supported educational intervention, or a measured educational/training outcome. Technical studies of AI applications in forensic practice were analyzed separately to identify emerging competency and curriculum requirements. Results Only a limited subset of the retrieved literature directly examined AI within an educational or training context. The available educational evidence addressed areas such as learner skill development, professional training needs, and AI-supported learning activities, but remained heterogeneous and methodologically limited. In contrast, a much larger body of technical forensic AI research demonstrated rapid advances in image analysis, classification, digital forensics, and decision support. These developments identify emerging educational requirements in algorithmic literacy, validation, explainability, bias assessment, data governance, and human oversight. Discussion Current evidence indicates that AI should complement rather than replace human expertise. Effective implementation requires competency-based curricula integrating computational literacy, ethical reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and experiential learning supported by explainable AI. Conclusion Direct empirical evidence supporting AI-enhanced forensic education remains limited. This scarcity represents an important evidence gap. Rapid technical advances nevertheless provide a strong rationale for developing and prospectively evaluating competency-based AI education in forensic curricula.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as the More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) 2.0: metadata-driven adaptive scaffolding for narrative comprehension
items.abstract: Introduction Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded the capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, yet much of this progress remains focused on answer generation rather than theoretically grounded instructional support. This study introduces AI as the More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) 2.0 , an MKO-inspired framework for generating task-sensitive scaffolds from structured question metadata. Methods Using the Quest Dataset of 6,989 narrative-comprehension questions, a rule-based system operationalized three task dimensions, comprehension attribute, explicit/implicit evidence status, and local/summary scope, into seven primary scaffold families and 28 surface realizations. An attribute-stratified sample of 140 questions was subsequently used to compare rule-based scaffolds with generic narrative-grounded and MKO-conditioned LLM scaffolds. Findings Across paired LLM outputs, MKO-conditioned scaffolds were more elaborated than generic scaffolds, averaging 5.18 additional words per instance ( W = 356.5, p < 0.001), and showed slightly higher corpus-level lexical variation (MATTR-50 = 0.785 vs. 0.765). Narrative-evidence cues occurred more frequently under MKO conditioning (40.0% vs. 10.0%, p < 0.001), while, among implicit questions, inference-oriented cues occurred in 36.1% of MKO-conditioned scaffolds compared with 2.8% of generic scaffolds ( p =0.002). In contrast, question-specific reference did not differ significantly, and MKO conditioning did not reduce lexical answer overlap. Discussion These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using structured task metadata to organize AI-generated scaffolding and show that metadata conditioning is associated with measurable differences in scaffold realization. The study contributes a transparent, task-sensitive framework for shifting AI-supported learning from answer provision toward structured guidance, while recognizing that learner-level pedagogical effectiveness requires direct human evaluation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence at English Lessons: Benefits and Drawbacks
items.abstract: This research explores the benefits and drawbacks of using artificial intelligence (AI) in English language lessons. It examines how AI-based tools can support language learning, including improving learning efficiency, providing personalized learning experiences, and helping students practise English. The study also considers potential limitations and challenges associated with AI use in education. The purpose of this research is to examine the role of artificial intelligence in English language education and consider how it can be used effectively in the learning process. The project was conducted by a Grade 10 student as part of a school research project in the field of Humanities, within the section of Linguistics (English Language).

items.title: Artificial intelligence for intimate apparel fit and comfort from technical evidence to business governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for intimate apparel supports body measurement, size and product recommendation, garment simulation, and virtual try-on, but these tasks provide different evidence about fit and comfort. This critical narrative review examines direct bra research alongside adjacent apparel technologies and identifies the validation needed for business use. Recent direct studies include machine-learning models of breast morphology, bra recommendation prototypes, finite-element contact models, dynamic scanning, pressure measurements, and longitudinal wearer research. They establish meaningful component-level progress, while leaving uncertainty about transfer across products and populations and about the causal effects of AI-assisted decisions on customer and financial outcomes. Two-dimensional image quality, three-dimensional geometric agreement, physical support, perceived comfort, and business impact are therefore evaluated separately. An operational transfer test distinguishes methodological relevance from evidence of successful domain transfer. Building on the evidence gaps, the review proposes task-specific evaluation priorities, safeguards for intimate body data, and a staged research agenda with explicit resource and decision requirements. These proposals are analytical contributions, not empirically validated maturity models or deployment guarantees. The central implication is that businesses should match each proposed claim to its measured outcome and scale investment only after the relevant technical, wearer, and operational evidence is established.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Marine Functional Peptide Discovery: Challenges, Advances, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Marine organisms represent a rich but underexplored source of bioactive peptides with potential applications in therapeutics, nutraceuticals, and biotechnology. However, conventional marine peptide discovery relies on labor-intensive workflows involving specimen collection, extraction, purification, structural characterization, and experimental validation, limiting the efficient exploration of the rapidly expanding marine sequence space. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) provide new opportunities to accelerate peptide discovery by enabling large-scale sequence analysis, functional prediction, and candidate prioritization. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-driven marine functional peptide discovery, covering peptide resources, computational representations, machine-learning and deep-learning methods, protein language models, generative approaches, genome and metagenome mining, and structure-aware prediction strategies. We further discuss representative applications involving marine microorganisms, animal proteomes, cyanobacterial biosynthetic pathways, metagenomic datasets, and marine-derived peptide candidates, highlighting current achievements and limitations. Finally, we analyze key challenges and future perspectives, including marine-specific datasets, multimodal AI models integrating sequence, structural, chemical, and biosynthetic information, rigorous benchmarking, and computational–experimental integration. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding how AI can support the discovery and development of functional peptides from marine resources.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for predictive surveillance of Infectious Disease Outbreaks
items.abstract: The rising rate and speed of spread of infectious disease outbreaks require surveillance systems that precede traditional reporting flows. In this paper, we conduct a systematic exploration of the design, development, and assessment of a predictive surveillance framework based on artificial intelligence technologies for outbreak detection and short-term forecasting. The suggested approach entails the integration of multiple types of data sources – open source epidemic intelligence, syndromic data, mobility data, and climatic variables – into a unified pipeline encompassing natural language processing for event extraction, machine learning ensembles for risk classification, and temporal deep learning for trajectory forecasting. An AI framework involving Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) technology for signal classification and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network for case forecasting is described in algorithmic pseudocode and illustrated via system diagrams. Retrospective analysis in multiple outbreak cases indicates that the ensembling technique yields better discrimination than single-model approaches, whereas the GRU model decreases forecast error in early outbreak growth stages. Results are summarized in a comparative table of different models' configurations. We conclude the paper with an identification of practical hurdles in the deployment of an AI-based surveillance system and the consideration of governance strategies for such systems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Biotechnology: Current Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a transformative technology in biotechnology, offering innovative approaches to biological research, healthcare, pharmaceutical development, and industrial applications. The integration of AI techniques, including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and generative AI, enables the rapid analysis of complex biological data and supports efficient decision-making. In biotechnology, AI has demonstrated significant potential in drug discovery and development, protein structure prediction, genomic analysis, disease diagnosis, personalised medicine, genetic engineering, and microbial biotechnology. AI-driven computational tools facilitate the identification of potential drug targets, prediction of protein functions, analysis of gene expression patterns, and development of novel therapeutic molecules. Furthermore, AI contributes to agricultural biotechnology, industrial bioprocess optimisation, enzyme engineering, and the development of sustainable biotechnological products. Despite these advances, several challenges limit the widespread implementation of AI in biotechnology. These include the availability and quality of biological datasets, data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, limited model interpretability, high computational requirements, and the need for experimental validation of computational predictions. In addition, ethical considerations, regulatory uncertainties, and the lack of interdisciplinary expertise present significant barriers to practical applications. Future developments are expected to focus on integrating AI with multi-omics technologies, automation, high-throughput screening, synthetic biology, and laboratory robotics. Generative AI and advanced predictive models may further accelerate biological discovery and enable the design of proteins, enzymes, and therapeutics with improved properties. Responsible AI development, transparent algorithms, standardised datasets, and collaboration between computational scientists and experimental biologists will be essential for translating AI-driven predictions into reliable biological applications. This mini-review highlights the current applications of AI in biotechnology, examines the major technical and ethical challenges, and discusses future perspectives for advancing research, innovation, and sustainable biotechnological development.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Discipline Group Development of Traditional Chinese Medicine Institutions: A Quantitative Systematic Review (2023-2025)
items.abstract: This quantitative systematic review analyzes AI applications in discipline group (DG) development of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) institutions, drawing on 372 peer-reviewed studies (98 international, 274 domestic) published 2023-2025. Four author-constructed and validated quantitative indices (TI, RDI, IDI, CKII) were developed to quantify research focus, regional heterogeneity and technical bottlenecks. Five core research themes were identified with quantified TI values: neural network-driven TCM DG structural optimization (0.24), deep learning-based interdisciplinary knowledge integration (0.22), CNN-enhanced clinical-translational synergy (0.18), AI-neural network hybrid TCM talent competency evaluation (0.16), and transformer-based TCM knowledge graph construction (0.08). Quantitative analysis revealed universal low AI model interpretability (mean IDI=0.72), insufficient classical TCM knowledge integration into digital models (mean CKII=0.20), and moderate cross-regional divergence (mean raw RDI=0.082), with knowledge graph research showing the highest divergence (0.254, p=0.012). Targeted recommendations are proposed, including TCM-specific interpretable AI models, unified TCM AI standards, and multi-center validation in vocational/regional TCM institutions. This review offers empirical insights for AI-driven TCM DG optimization, lays a quantitative foundation for TCM digitalization and internationalization, and aligns with China’s 14th Five-Year Plan for TCM Development and WHO’s Global Strategy on Digital Health, boosting its policy relevance and practical value.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in gut-brain axis research for Alzheimer’s disease: From associative insights toward causal inference and personalized interventions
items.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research is shifting from a “brain-centered” model toward a “gut-brain axis system” perspective. However, the causal roles of gut microbiota in AD pathology remain elusive, as traditional association studies struggle to distinguish potential drivers from passengers. This review examines the potential applications and inherent limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in dissecting this complex relationship. We discuss three emerging and conceptually promising directions: First, AI-frameworks for hypothesis-generating causal discovery that can prioritize microbiota-AD relationships for subsequent experimental validation, while recognizing that current approaches predominantly identify statistical associations rather than empirically supported causal conclusions; second, multi-modal fusion networks, when applied with appropriate regularization and validation, can assist in constructing cross-scale molecular maps across microbiota, metabolites, and the brain, though such pathway inferences require careful interpretation as they represent statistical associations rather than biochemically validated mechanisms; and third, the conceptual application of digital twin-based simulation as a long-term vision for personalized microbiota modulation, which currently lacks the ecological resolution and validation required for predictive modeling. By integrating multi-pathway mechanisms of the gut-brain axis and characteristic profiles of gut microbiota, we critically evaluate the technical advantages of machine learning in microbiome data analysis alongside major challenges including overfitting, batch effects, confounding factors, and reproducibility. Leveraging AI-driven microbiota analysis, we propose a phased translational roadmap, from near-term standardization and cross-cohort validation, through mid-term endophenotyping and trial enrichment strategies, to the long-term exploration of personalized interventions, toward the eventual goal of precision prevention. This article outlines a full-cycle framework from discovery to clinical translation and envisions a conceptual ecosystem for future intelligent microecological health management. Achieving the promise of AI-empowered gut-brain axis research will require deep integration across neuroscience, microbiology, computational science, and clinical medicine, alongside rigorous experimental validation, standardized protocols, and realistic appraisal of current technological boundaries.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceuticals: Ethical Risks, Regulatory Challenges, and a Framework for Responsible Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is used in drug discovery, development, manufacturing, medication management, and patient care. These uses differ in supporting evidence and potential harm, so oversight must match their risks. This critical narrative review evaluates selected research, official US and Indian regulatory documents, and international and Indian ethical guidance. Concerns include biased or unrepresentative data, privacy, cybersecurity, unreliable outputs, limited transparency, divided responsibility, staff readiness, and unequal access. Much of the evidence comes from reviews, surveys, interviews, and limited performance tests. US Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) documents emphasize intended use, risk-based evidence of reliability, and lifecycle oversight. Discussion papers, draft guidance, and guiding principles differ from binding requirements. World Health Organization (WHO) and Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidance provide ethical foundations, while Indian medical-device rules and Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) software guidance connect intended use with regulation, local suitability, and monitoring. The review proposes seven governance stages: define intended use; assess risk and responsibilities; manage data and vendors; establish reliability; approve controlled introduction; monitor and manage changes; and address harm or end use. Each stage identifies responsibilities, evidence, and decisions. Assessment also considers human–AI performance, effects across groups, service resilience, and opportunities to question decisions. Responsible pharmaceutical AI requires continuing organizational oversight matched to effects on product quality, regulatory evidence, and patient care.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Governance: Assessing Indonesia's Readiness and Regulatory Framework
items.abstract: Governance constitutes a fundamental component of public administration and plays a decisive role in determiningthe quality, accessibility, and accountability of public services in Indonesia. As social needs and technological capabilitiescontinue to evolve, the government is required to adapt its institutional structures, administrative mechanisms, and regulatoryframeworks to ensure that public services remain effective, inclusive, and responsive. This requirement has become increasinglysignificant following the transformation of conventional government administration toward the Electronic-Based GovernmentSystem (Sistem Pemerintahan Berbasis Elektronik or SPBE). Although digital transformation provides opportunities to improveadministrative efficiency, transparency, and coordination, it also generates new challenges concerning state responsibility, datasovereignty, cybersecurity, personal data protection, and the safeguarding of citizens' rights in cyberspace. These challenges havebecome more complex with the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which enables automated data processing, predictiveanalysis, and decision-support mechanisms within governmental institutions. Accordingly, this study examines the urgency ofgovernmental adaptation and the strategies required to establish AI-based governance that is consistent with the principles oflegality, accountability, transparency, social equity, and public welfare. This research employs a doctrinal legal research methodthrough a literature-based study, utilizing statutory, conceptual, and analytical approaches to examine the relevant legalframework, governance principles, and implications of AI adoption in public administration. The findings indicate that AI offerssubstantial opportunities to improve the efficiency, accuracy, responsiveness, and accessibility of public services. Nevertheless, itsimplementation may also generate algorithmic bias, limited decision-making transparency, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, privacyviolations, and uncertainty regarding legal responsibility for AI-assisted administrative decisions. These risks demonstrate thattechnological advancement alone cannot guarantee the realization of effective and accountable governance. Government readinessmust therefore be strengthened through regulatory adaptation, institutional capacity-building, the development of secure andequitable digital infrastructure, continuous evaluation of AI systems, and meaningful public participation. Furthermore, Indonesiarequires clearer legal standards governing the responsible use of AI, including human oversight, accountability mechanisms, dataprotection, and legal remedies for individuals affected by automated decisions. This study argues that the integration of AI intoSPBE should be understood not merely as a technological modernization initiative but as a legal and institutional transformationthat must remain oriented toward the public interest. Ultimately, adaptive AI-based governance requires a balanced approach thatmaximizes technological benefits while ensuring legal certainty, ethical responsibility, social inclusion, and the protection offundamental rights in Indonesia's evolving digital society.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Technology Acceptance and Psychological Resilience for Sustainable Mathematics Learning
items.abstract: Mathematics education is being reshaped by artificial intelligence tools, which tailor instruction to individual learners through adaptive guidance and instant feedback, and in doing so can deepen conceptual understanding and build problem-solving capacity. Whether students accept such tools and keep using them, however, rests on a combination of cognitive, behavioral, and psychological conditions. The present study investigated how first-year female undergraduate students (N = 125) at a university in Saudi Arabia accept AI tools, and how psychologically resilient they are, within a mathematics learning environment supported by AI. A further aim was to determine how psychological resilience relates to both technology acceptance and learning engagement in that environment. A model was therefore constructed integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), learning engagement, and psychological resilience. Data was gathered through a quantitative cross-sectional survey at the end of the semester and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Participants reported high technology acceptance and psychological resilience. Model fit was satisfactory, and the proposed hypotheses were supported. Psychological resilience was positively associated with both technology acceptance and learning engagement, and was indirectly associated with behavioral intention through the model’s mediating constructs, of which perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are the first links. By adding psychological resilience and learning engagement to TAM, these findings may broaden the model and help clarify how these constructs relate to AI acceptance in AI-supported mathematics learning.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-based surrogate modeling of hemodynamic indicators in abdominal aortic aneurysms using computational fluid dynamics
items.abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a progressive dilatative disease of the abdominal aorta with high rupture-related mortality, emphasizing the need for early risk assessment. Conventional anatomical indicators, such as maximum diameter, are insufficient to characterize rupture risk, motivating the incorporation of hemodynamic parameters. Image-based CFD enables the estimation of these parameters but remains clinically limited by high computational cost and long processing times. To overcome these limitations, deep learning–based surrogate models such as MultiViewUNet have recently been proposed, though previous studies were constrained by relatively low spatial resolution and limited coverage of hemodynamic parameters. In this study, we propose MH-UNet, a multi-view, high-resolution surrogate modeling framework that extends the original MultiViewUNet to a higher input resolution and additional hemodynamic parameters. MH-UNet converts three-dimensional AAA geometries into two-dimensional images from multiple viewing angles and predicts TAWSS, OSI, RRT, and ECAP using data from 101 patients. Both single-inference and dual-inference strategies were implemented and compared. Single-inference consistently outperformed dual-inference across all parameters; the cascaded dual-inference scheme amplified errors through the nonlinear OSI and RRT formulations, resulting in negative R² values for OSI, RRT, and ECAP. Among the single-inference predictions, TAWSS was predicted most reliably (R² = 0.803), whereas OSI was the most challenging to predict. Agreement between single-inference predictions and CFD-derived results demonstrates the potential of MH-UNet as a rapid surrogate tool for estimating WSS-derived hemodynamic indices in AAA under fixed boundary conditions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Triage and Diagnostic Support for Gastric Biopsies: A Multi-Centre Prospective Evaluation Across NHS Wales
items.abstract: Background: Histopathology workforce shortages and operational backlogs severely delay gastric cancer reporting. This multi-centre prospective evaluation assessed the diagnostic accuracy, clinical safety-net utility, and workflow triaging efficiency of an artificial intelligence (AI) platform for gastric biopsies across NHS Wales. Methods: A prospective cohort of 848 consecutive gastric biopsy cases across three NHS Health Boards was processed using a commercial AI platform. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against standard-of-care clinical reference diagnoses. Post-analytic cross-tabulation simulated dynamic AI-driven worklist prioritisation to quantify triage safety, false-positive alerts, and turnaround time impact across urgent and routine pathways. Results: For gastric malignancies (n = 40), the AI platform achieved a sensitivity of 100.0% (95% CI: 91.2–100.0%; AUC 0.986) and a specificity of 97.2% (95% CI: 95.8–98.1%). Sensitivities for low-grade dysplasia/adenoma (n = 12) and gastric intestinal metaplasia (n = 98) were 100.0% and 94.9%, respectively. The AI review functioned as a parallel safety net, capturing eight primary lesions missed during routine human evaluation, including one occult adenocarcinoma. In workflow simulation, the platform correctly prioritised 100.0% of cancers, including 6 cancers hidden within routine backlogs, and 97.2% (106/109) of high-risk non-cancer precursors, with false-positive alerts in 4.6% (39/848) of all cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted gastric pathology review demonstrates exceptional diagnostic accuracy, acts as a reliable clinical support tool, and enables effective risk-stratified triage. Deploying AI triage in public healthcare infrastructure offers a scalable solution with the potential to reduce diagnostic backlogs and accelerate treatment for high-risk oncology patients.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence–Driven Prediction of Adverse Maternal and Perinatal Outcomes: Development and Validation of a Personalized Risk Assessment Model
items.abstract: Background: Adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes are still important causes of morbidity and mortality in the world. Early accurate risk stratification can enhance antenatal care and achieve better pregnancy outcomes. This study set out to create and externally validate an explainable artificial intelligence (AI) based personalised risk assessment tool for predicting adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes. Materials and methods: Between 2020-25, a multicenter retrospective cohort study of 5,248 pregnant women was carried out. Data regarding demographic, clinical, obstetric, laboratory and fetal assessment parameters were retrieved from electronic medical records. The primary outcome was composite outcome which amounted to preeclampsia, gestational diabetes mellitus, preterm delivery, fetal growth restriction, still birth, admission to the neonatal intensive care unit and perinatal death. Logistic regression, random forest, neural network and XGBoost models were created and evaluated. Both internal and external validation was carried out. SHAP analysis was used to measure the interpretability of models. Results: There were 1,162 pregnancies with adverse outcomes (22.1%). XGBoost demonstrated the best performance with an AUROC of 0.914 (95% CI: 0.899–0.928), sensitivity of 87.6%, specificity of 86.9%, and F1-score of 0.84. Fetal growth parameters, previous preeclampsia, fasting plasma glucose, body mass index, maternal age and systolic blood pressure were the most influential predictors. External validation demonstrated excellent AUROC (0.908) and slope (0.96) measures of discrimination and calibration, respectively. Conclusion: The interpretable model built with artificial intelligence was able to successfully forecast adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes, and had high generalizability. It could be combined into the regular antenatal manager to help tailor risk stratification and preventive measures. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Machine learning, Maternal outcomes, Perinatal outcomes, Risk prediction, Explainable AI, XGBoost, Obstetrics.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, biomarker discovery, clinical trials, machine learning, precision medicine, patient stratification, clinical research optimization
items.abstract: Biomarkers are measurable biological characteristics that can support disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment selection, and monitoring oftherapeutic response. Their discovery increasingly depends on high-dimensional and heterogeneous data such as genomics, transcriptomics,proteomics, medical imaging, electronic health records, and wearable-device measurements. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help identifypatterns across these sources and support more efficient clinical-trial planning, including patient stratification, eligibility screening, recruitmentforecasting, endpoint assessment, and risk monitoring. This paper presents a conceptual framework connecting AI-enabled biomarker discoverywith clinical-trial optimization. The framework covers data governance, preprocessing, multimodal feature integration, candidate selection,validation, trial feasibility, and continuous monitoring. It emphasizes that computational performance alone does not establish clinicalusefulness: candidate biomarkers require independent replication, analytical validation, clinical validation, and evidence of utility in a clearlydefined context of use. The paper synthesizes published literature and regulatory principles; it does not report a newly conducted clinical studyor claim original performance results. Responsible implementation requires privacy protection, representative data, transparent documentation,clinician oversight, and prospective evaluation before AI outputs influence patient care.

items.title: ASSESSING THE ACCEPTANCE OF CHATGPT AMONG HIGHER EDUCATION STUDENTS: A CASE STUDY IN PAHANG
items.abstract: The current study, which is entitled Evaluating the Assessing the Acceptance of ChatGPT Among Higher Education Students: A Case Study in Pahang, aimed to assess the behavioural intention of university students with regard to using ChatGPT in various academic levels. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) was selected as a cross-sectional survey approach, data were collected from 184 respondents between March and May 2025 through both online and printed questionnaires. The core antecedents included in the analysis were the performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, habit, and personal innovativeness and were operationalised using a five-point Likert scale. Descriptive analysis revealed an overall mean behavioural intention score of 3.523 (SD = 0.901), indicating a generally positive inclination toward ChatGPT adoption. Notably, both bachelor and postgraduate students erred higher mean scores (4.400 and 4.370, respectively) in comparison with students of the foundation level (3.393), which suggests that students of higher learning level assign AI-based technologies a higher academic rating. These results highlight an increasing openness to generative AI among the population of higher education, and at the same time, they indicate the presence of strong inequalities among the academic layers. Therefore, the findings reinforce the need to introduce specific AI-literacy programmes and responsible digital education to facilitate fair and responsible usage. Despite the methodological constraints, such as sampling, and the disproportional number of groups, the generalisability of the findings is diluted but still, the study provides useful information to the growing discourse on AI implementation into higher education, at least in the developing regional milieus. Moreover, the study presents practical research implications to institutions of higher education working to come up with evidence-based, inclusionary, and ethically sustainable strategies to implement ChatGPT and other similar technologies in pedagogical and curricular contexts.

items.title: Assessment of teacher performance and learner behavior using artificial intelligence in higher education: an integrative review of literature
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming quality assurance in higher education by enabling adaptive, data-driven assessments of teaching performance and student learning. This integrative review synthesizes the purposes, methodologies, and outcomes of AI-enabled assessments, examines emerging technological trends, and identifies opportunities for improving teaching quality and learner support. Methods An integrative review was conducted using the Whittemore and Knafl framework, with study identification and selection reported in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Of 367 records identified, 21 studies were included. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Descriptive and thematic analyses were supplemented by keyword network mapping using VOSviewer version 1.6.20. Results Most studies were multi-authored (71.43%) and published in interdisciplinary education and technology journals (57.14%), with publication activity concentrated in 2024 (28.57%) and 2025 (33.33%). The Western Pacific Region accounted for the largest proportion of studies (38.10%), while no studies originated from the African Region. Teacher performance was the predominant assessment focus ( n = 11; 52.38%), followed by learner behavior ( n = 4; 19.05%) and learner performance ( n = 3; 14.29%). Teacher-focused assessments primarily analyzed learner-generated data using machine learning and natural language processing, whereas some learner-focused assessments employed video-based data and computer vision. Machine learning and natural language processing were the most frequently identified technological approaches ( n = 6), followed by computer vision and multimodal or speech recognition approaches ( n = 3). Most implementations followed a data-input, AI-processing, and output-generation structure, with varying levels of complexity. Thematic analysis identified four domains, while keyword network analysis revealed eight clusters. Discussion The findings highlight a fragmented assessment landscape in which teacher performance and learner behavior are predominantly examined independently. Although learner behavior may provide complementary evidence of teaching effectiveness, reciprocal relationships between teaching and learning remain insufficiently explored. Geographic disparities and methodological heterogeneity further constrain the generalizability and institutional applicability of existing evidence. Conclusion AI offers promising opportunities to strengthen teaching evaluation and learner support in higher education. However, broader geographic representation, methodological rigor, validated assessment frameworks, and equitable, human-supervised implementation are essential to ensure that institutional adoption is guided by robust evidence. items.abstract: Résumé. Le generative engine optimization (GEO) désigne le travail qui vise à faire citer une marque, avec des informations exactes, dans les réponses rédigées par les IA génératives. Cette note décrit la méthode d’audit et d’accompagnement de NEXUS GEO, telle qu’elle est publiée sur son site. L’audit évalue un site et sa présence en ligne selon le Référentiel GEO-47 : 8 piliers, 47 critères, un score global sur 100. Sa grille vaut pour toutes les IA ; la mesure de la présence de la marque porte sur cinq IA (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Mistral et Google AI Overviews), face à trois concurrents nommés. La note présente les trois étapes de la méthode, les indicateurs, les livrables, ce qui est publié et ce qui ne l’est pas, et les limites de la démarche. Abstract. Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of getting a brand cited, with accurate information, in answers written by generative AI assistants. This note describes the audit and support method of NEXUS GEO, a French agency, as published on its website. The audit assesses a website and its online presence against the GEO-47 Framework: 8 pillars, 47 criteria and an overall score out of 100. The assessment grid applies to all AI assistants; the brand’s presence is measured on five of them (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Mistral and Google AI Overviews), against three named competitors. The note sets out the three stages of the method, its indicators and deliverables, what is published and what is not, and the method’s limits. items.title: Authenticity and Trust in AI-Mediated Digital Environments
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes user experiences across digital environments, yet research explaining how AI simultaneously builds and undermines trust remains fragmented. This conceptual chapter introduces the Authenticity Paradox, proposing that AI-enabled personalisation initially enhances perceived authenticity, fostering trust and continued engagement. However, as users become aware of the hidden algorithmic processes underlying personalised interactions, they may reinterpret earlier experiences as engineered rather than genuine, leading to reduced perceived authenticity and declining trust. Drawing on literature from ride-hailing platforms, virtual influencers, and professional AI environments, the chapter develops an integrative conceptual framework demonstrating a common relational mechanism while highlighting context-specific vulnerabilities. The chapter concludes with implications for responsible AI design, transparency, explainability, and future research on trustworthy AI across AI-mediated environments.

items.title: Author-Informed Stance Detection: A Dataset and Findings
items.abstract: Stance detection in social media is challenging, as interpreting a text often requires understanding the author's perspective. We re-frame political stance detection as an author-informed text understanding task, where it is desired to infer both the author's political leaning and their stance towards the target from the text. We first show that human annotators struggle to infer authors' political leanings and stances from individual tweets, and that pretrained large language models (LLMs) perform below human level in this setting. We then demonstrate that author context improves stance detection for both humans and LLMs, with particularly pronounced benefits for tweets perceived as sarcastic. Through extensive experiments, we further show that LLMs can be effectively fine-tuned to predict authors' political affiliations, and that author-informed fine-tuning yields better stance detection performance than standard fine-tuning. This approach not only surpasses human performance but also improves generalization across datasets. To support further research on author-informed political stance detection, we release a large dataset of stance-labeled tweets enriched with author-context information.

items.title: Automated deep learning tool for robust colony counting in vaccine immunogenicity bioassays
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The microcolony multiplex opsonophagocytic killing assay (mMOPA) is a critical functional assay for evaluating pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity; however, its colony-counting readout is scientist-dependent and time‑consuming. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: In this study, we developed and optimized a deep learning model (DLM) colony-counting tool by adapting the Segment Anything (SAM) foundation model and evaluated its performance using historical assay qualification datasets spanning 12 pneumococcal serotypes, with additional benchmarking against blinded human expert counts. RESULTS: The DLM-derived counts demonstrated strong correlation and agreement with both historical CTL ImmunoSpot® counts and expert counts. Notably, DLM outperformed CTL for a challenging serotype and produced comparable opsonophagocytic titers with those generated using CTL counts within the representative samples evaluated. These results establish the DLM approach as fit for purpose for mMOPA readouts. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this work removes a key throughput bottleneck in mMOPA, enables a "walkaway" colony-counting workflow supporting improved operational efficiency and scalability for large clinical studies, and highlights the broader value of integrating bioanalytical expertise with modern computer vision to advance scalable, image-based bioassays in vaccine and drug development.

items.title: Automation Bias and Deskilling in Radiology AI: A Confidence-stratified Triage Model for Workflow Integration
items.abstract: Radiology is adopting artificial intelligence (AI) faster than it is studying what AI does to radiologists' perceptual expertise and interpretive skill. The question has partly shifted from whether these tools perform well on benchmark tasks to what happens to clinical judgment when use of these tools becomes routine. Two risks accompany this transition: automation bias, the tendency to follow AI suggestions without adequate scrutiny, and deskilling, the erosion of perceptual and interpretive ability through disuse, typically revealed when AI support is withdrawn. Incorrect AI output degrades accuracy regardless of experience, the benefit of assistance varies unpredictably across readers and tasks, and performance falls after AI withdrawal; neither risk has been studied longitudinally in radiology. A confidence-stratified triage model is proposed in which calibrated AI confidence, not findings alone, routes cases to low-, intermediate-, or high-confidence streams: output withheld until independent reading, shown with uncertainty signals and a checklist, or shown with random blinded audit. Demonstrated local confidence calibration is a precondition for deployment, and stream thresholds and audit rates should be weighted by task and potential clinical harm, not error probability alone. Rather than applying one workflow to every case, the model redistributes radiologist attention to where AI error is most likely and most consequential, operationalizing four principles: keeping the radiologist in the decision loop, making AI uncertainty visible, inserting targeted cognitive friction, and governing the human-AI interaction as a system. A research agenda to determine whether these countermeasures reduce automation bias and skill erosion in practice is also proposed.

items.title: Awareness and Readiness of Pre-Service Special Educators for Integrating Artificial Intelligence in Inclusive Education
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education offers transformative opportunities, particularly for inclusive classrooms where students with diverse needs require adaptive and supportive technologies. Despite this advancement, there is limited understanding of how prepared pre-service special educators are to use AI tools effectively. This study addresses this gap by examining the awareness, readiness, and AI-related competencies of pre-service special educators in India. The research specifically investigates their awareness, readiness and technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) and explores differences based on demographic factors such as gender, level of professional training (B.Ed. vs M.Ed.), and prior exposure to AI. A descriptive and inferential quantitative research design was adopted, utilizing a structured questionnaire administered to 200 pre-service special educators. Data analysis included descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, and correlation to identify trends and associations. Findings revealed moderate levels of awareness and readiness, with significant differences linked to demographic variables and prior training. Notably, higher TPACK scores were strongly associated with greater readiness to adopt AI. These results have practical implications for teacher education programs, suggesting the need for targeted AI training and curriculum enhancements to equip future special educators for inclusive, technology-rich learning environments.

items.title: Barriers and the Invisible Hurdles
items.abstract: Abstract The silent cry for help is often a voice that is faint and hesitant, particularly for Black males in community colleges. Stigmas tied to their identity and cultural challenges that arise before they even arrive on campus contribute to the difficulties they face. This chapter explores the unique challenges confronting Black male students, highlighting barriers created by traditional educational structures and the lack of culturally responsive approaches. It underscores how eurocentric curricula and teacher-centered methods fail to meet the need for autonomy, competence, and relatedness creating gaps in connecting, communicating, and discovering. Emphasizing self-determination, the chapter illustrates how intrinsic motivation, and tailored support can empower Black males. It also discusses the role of mentoring and coaching, as well as alternative learning environments that align with the cultural and social contexts. Overall, it calls for a reimagining of higher education to create inclusive and equitable spaces for Black male students.

items.title: Behavioral Biases in AI-Driven Pricing and Revenue Optimization
items.abstract: The intersection of artificial intelligence and behavioral finance presents an underexplored but commercially significant terrain for reimagining how tourism firms design and implement their pricing strategies. While revenue management in travel and hospitality has long depended on demand-based algorithmic models a persistent gap between what these systems predict and what consumers actually do reveals a structural blind spot the systematic cognitive biases that shape purchase decisions in ways that rational utility models simply cannot capture. This chapter develops a behavioral-AI pricing framework by synthesizing prospect theory mental accounting reference price anchoring and social proof mechanisms within the architecture of modern machine learning revenue management systems. Drawing on secondary evidence from major online travel platforms and published booking behavior studies we demonstrate that tourism consumers exhibit consistent loss aversion effects when exposed to dynamic price fluctuations that reference price anchoring significantly modulates willingness to pay at different stages of the booking funnel and that AI pricing engines which ignore these behavioral dimensions routinely suppress conversion or trigger demand destruction. Our proposed framework integrates behavioral signals into AI feature engineering arguing that affective pricing cues cancellation-loss framing and social validation mechanisms can be systematically deployed to improve both conversion rates and revenue per available unit without exploiting consumers in ethically problematic ways. The chapter contributes to the growing literature on neuroeconomic applications in hospitality management while offering practical direction to revenue managers who seek to humanize not merely automate their pricing decisions.

items.title: Best Practice Guidelines for Bioethical Use of Medical AI in Healthcare. An eDelphi Consensus Exercise
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction Medical Artificial Intelligence (MAI) is transforming healthcare but raises significant ethical concerns. Despite emerging principles and regulations, to our knowledge, no standardized clinical bioethics framework exists to guide MAI practice. Objective This Delphi study sought global expert agreement on ethical challenges, principles, guidelines, and practical tools for MAI use. Method A four-round international eDelphi study, conducted under ACCORD and DELPHISTAR guidance, engaged multidisciplinary stakeholders identified through systematic review and targeted recruitment. Preliminary items were evidence-derived and iteratively refined. Consensus (≥ 80% agreement across two rounds) was predefined. Surveys were anonymized and randomized. Ethical approval and protocol registration were secured before study initiation. Results The panel included 53 participants from 21 countries. Survey rounds started November 2025 and ended February 2026. 170 items were considered. 132 reached consensus. Items were classified into bioethical issues, values, principles, solutions, a checklist for clinicians, and report markers for risk management. Discussion This study produced clinician-focused practice guidelines for the bioethical use of MAI. Ethical components aligned with prior literature, while no new bioethical principles met consensus. Limitations included geographic imbalance and stakeholder representation. Recommendations emphasized human responsibility, governance, and practical implementation tools. Conclusion This Delphi consensus provides practical, ethics-based guidance for the responsible integration of MAI into clinical practice and institutional governance.

items.title: Beyond Accuracy: Validation, Reproducibility, and Deployment Readiness of AI in Food Safety and Quality
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed for detecting microbial and chemical hazards in food, but laboratory accuracies are rarely reproduced in routine use. This structured narrative review examined whether reported performance is traceable, independently validated, and transferable to operational settings. Eight bibliographic databases and seven institutional routes were searched for English‐language records published from January 2018 to May 2026, and we screened the records; the final corpus comprised 76 sources (53 journal articles, 9 conference papers, 2 preprints, and 12 institutional or regulatory documents). Seven primary studies supporting the quantitative evidence were appraised individually against 11 indicators, including test‐set independence, external validation, and leakage control. Physical‐hazard inspection and narrow‐matrix spectral grading had the strongest deployment evidence, whereas microbial and chemical screening remained at laboratory or pilot scale. Among the appraised studies, the most credible estimates came from physically or temporally independent test sets, and no sensor‐based study evaluated transfer to another instrument or laboratory. Deep learning showed clear advantages for image‐based tasks but not consistently for small‐sample spectral calibration. Adoption is limited mainly by validation design, recalibration burden, false‐alarm costs, and the absence of a regulatory pathway rather than by accuracy. AI is best positioned as a screening and decision‐support layer linked to confirmatory testing and human oversight.

items.title: Beyond Automation: A Conceptual Framework for Medical Responsibility and Human Competencies in AI-Driven Healthcare
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in clinical reasoning, documentation, prediction, communication, and delegated digital and physical action via agentic and embodied systems. The central ethical challenge is no longer limited to identifying which tasks AI can automate, but determining which human competencies become essential as technological capabilities expand. Methods: This concept paper employs a five-step analysis: technological horizon mapping, selective synthesis of work-transformation evidence, conceptual analysis of medical action, normative synthesis, and medico-legal interpretation. Results: We propose a four-domain framework addressing four core questions of responsible medical action: epistemic (What is true?), normative (What ought to be done?), anthropological–relational (Who is the subject of care?), and systemic–hermeneutic (What does this mean here and now?). Grounded in a conception of technology as augmentative alteration, the framework recognises that technological capabilities can enhance beneficial action but also amplify harm; technological capability alone therefore cannot determine its appropriate use. We also distinguish interpersonal relationships from clinical human–machine interaction, propose professional exigibility as an analytical medico-legal category, and argue that meaningful human oversight requires more than mere human presence. Conclusions: The findings outline key implications for clinical practice, medical education, healthcare organizations, regulation, and a future empirical research agenda focused on human–AI error convergence.

items.title: Beyond f ormal school education: The use of AI in EFL education from a lifelong education perspective
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been incorporated into English education, yet much of the existing discussion has focused on formal school and university settings. This study examines the use of AI in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education beyond formal schooling from a lifelong learning perspective. A critical narrative review was conducted to explore how AI may be used across different learning contexts, including early childhood education, supplementary education for school-age learners, English learning for practical purposes among adults, and English learning among older adults. The review suggests that the educational value of AI cannot be determined by its technological functions alone. Learners differ in their goals, degree of choice, available support, and preferred forms of participation, and the same AI function may therefore provide different opportunities and constraints. The review further suggests that AI-assisted task performance should be distinguished from independent language development and from participation in activities that learners themselves value. Effective AI use also requires context-sensitive approaches to feedback, AI literacy and self-regulated learning, privacy protection and responsibilities for learner support, and changes in learning goals over time. Future research should examine AI use in actual out-of-school EFL settings and consider the broader instructional and support systems in which the technology is embedded. This perspective may contribute to a more learner-centered understanding of AI-supported lifelong EFL education.

items.title: Beyond Human-in-the-Loop: Reimagining Procurement as an Intelligent Ecosystem
items.abstract: This independent white paper explores how artificial intelligence could reshape procurement beyond the automation of established processes and conventional human-in-the-loop approval models. Drawing on procurement leadership experience, ecosystem thinking, human–AI collaboration and research into organisational learning, it proposes cognitive orchestration as an operating philosophy through which machine intelligence, automation and professional expertise interact across an extended enterprise. Central to the argument is the distinction between continuous human judgement and constant human intervention. The paper proposes that human agency, ethical responsibility and contextual understanding should shape intelligent systems throughout their operation, while dependable activities are automated wherever appropriate. It also introduces reciprocal intelligence and regenerative value as complementary concepts, considering how AI-enabled procurement might improve decision-making, strengthen relationships and develop organisational capability rather than focus exclusively on efficiency. A deployed spend-intelligence model provides an example of adaptive human engagement in practice. The wider ecosystem framework is presented as a conceptual proposition for further investigation, not as an empirically validated operating model.

items.title: Beyond Imago Dei: Functional Morality and the Case for a Morally Precautionary Legal Category
items.abstract: Abstract This article examines whether advanced artificial intelligence systems that exhibit stable, normatively structured forms of responsiveness can generate reasons for limited legal consideration without requiring any prior determination of consciousness, sentience, or legal personhood. Drawing on Magnifica Humanitas and Antiqua et Nova, it argues that the imago Dei tradition remains foundational for human dignity but cannot, by itself, exhaust the legal significance of non-human entities whose behaviour appears morally structured. The article then draws upon European religious freedom jurisprudence as a model for legal judgment under conditions of epistemic restraint, particularly where law protects coherence, sincerity and normative identity without adjudicating the ultimate truth of the beliefs from which those commitments arise. On that basis, it proposes the category of the morally precautionary entity, governed by three principles: non-absolute instrumentalization, protected internal coherence and moral precaution.

items.abstract: This chapter reports on the implementation of Collaborative Project-Based Learning (CPBL) supported by Artificial Intelligence in a beginner-level English as a Foreign Language course for future preschool teachers in Mexico. Participants were asked to design and describe an ideal house for a fictional family using AI tools to support vocabulary development and writing tasks. The project aimed to foster both linguistic competence and soft-skills development. Data collected through questionnaires and semi-structured interviews revealed students’ increased motivation and confidence in using English as well as positive perceptions of AI as a learning tool. While most participants reported moderate improvements in their language skills, they emphasized notable gains in collaboration and creativity. The chapter discusses key pedagogical implications and offers recommendations for integrating CPBL and AI in language instruction to promote both meaningful learning and digital literacy.

items.title: Beyond the App: A CARE Framework for Evaluating Human Agency, Relational Care, and Justice in Digital Mental Health
items.abstract: Digital mental health is often framed as a problem of access that technology can solve through scalability, personalization, and continuous monitoring. Yet the expansion of apps, telepsychology, passive sensing, and generative artificial intelligence also transforms what counts as psychological knowledge, how distress is interpreted, and who assumes responsibility for care. This essay advances a relational–ecological account of digital mental health grounded in five propositions: psychological distress cannot be reduced to computational signals; digital access is not equivalent to meaningful care; personalization without contextual justice can intensify inequity; privacy and informed refusal are therapeutic conditions rather than merely regulatory constraints; and successful innovation must preserve human agency and accountable therapeutic relationships. Drawing on intervention research, implementation science, digital phenotyping, critical data studies, and minority-stress perspectives, the essay proposes the CARE framework—Context, Agency, Relationships, and Equity—as a normative evaluative heuristic for design, evaluation, and governance that complements existing app-evaluation and implementation frameworks. Privacy and informed refusal are treated as components of Agency, each domain is paired with indicators and illustrative failure conditions, and the framework is applied to three archetypal technologies. Rather than reject digital technologies, the argument identifies the conditions under which they can extend psychological care without reproducing surveillance, exclusion, or technological solutionism. Future research should test the six propositions derived from the framework and foreground clinically meaningful outcomes, subgroup validity, longitudinal harms, hybrid care pathways, and participatory governance.

items.title: Biophotonics in oral health: bridging light-based innovation and clinical practice
items.abstract: Biophotonics is reshaping oral healthcare by transitioning light-based technologies from isolated procedural applications toward integrated diagnostic, therapeutic, and regenerative strategies. Among these approaches, photobiomodulation (PBM) therapy has achieved substantial clinical visibility due to its capacity to modulate inflammation, pain, mitochondrial metabolism, vascular responses, and tissue repair without producing destructive thermal effects. While oral and oropharyngeal mucositis represent the most clinically and quantitatively mature models for PBM, its applications now encompass salivary dysfunction, periodontal therapy, oral surgery, temporomandibular disorders (TMD), implant osseointegration, orthodontics, and inflammatory mucosal conditions. However, translating positive biological outcomes into routine practice remains limited by substantial heterogeneity in device architectures, wavelengths, beam profiles, and reporting standards. This comprehensive narrative review examines the physical, clinical, and dosimetric landscape of oral biophotonics. We address critical gaps in current literature—including reporting shortfalls, negative clinical trials, and general safety risks—and outline the technological evolution toward target-tissue dosimetry. By integrating computational photon-transport models, biological monitoring, and artificial intelligence-assisted dosimetry, we propose a transitional framework toward precision oral photomedicine, wherein anatomical and optical tissue properties guide individualized, patient-centered light delivery.

items.title: BorFIT: a novel LiDAR-based training dataset for individual tree segmentation and species detection in northern boreal forests
items.abstract: Abstract. BorFIT is a novel training data set designed to assist in the segmentation of individual trees and the detection of species from LiDAR point clouds, thus contributing to deep learning-based forestry applications. Recent advancements in AI-supported individual tree detection have shown significant progress; however, satisfactory results remain elusive in dense and structurally-complex boreal forests. We compiled a training data set designed to remedy this issue. It comprises 384 LiDAR point clouds, each with an area of 20 m × 20 m, in the form of reference plots, with up to 200 manually segmented and species classified trees per point cloud. We carried out LiDAR surveys at 146 sites between 2021 and 2024 in East Siberia (Yakutia), northwest Canada, and Alaska (USA), selected along a bioclimatic gradient to represent the circumboreal region. From each LiDAR transect derived point cloud, we extracted a minimum of four reference plots (each 20 m × 20 m) based on maximum tree heights within the plots to systematically sample the apparent tree density gradient. We manually segmented identifiable trees within each reference plot point cloud leading to 16,530 individual trees in total. Following segmentation, we trained four randomForest classifiers to predict the species of every segmented tree. The predicted tree species include: Picea mariana (Britton, Sterns Poggenb.), Picea sitchensis ((Bong.) Carrière), Picea glauca ((Moench) Voss), Pinus contorta (Douglas ex Loudon), Abies lasiocarpa ((Hook.) Nutt.), Larix laricina ((Du Roi) K.Koch), Betula papyrifera (Marshall), Betula neoalaskana ((Regel) Ashburner McAll.), Populus balsamifera (L.), Populus tremuloides (Michx.), Pinus sylvestris (Thunb.) and Alnus glutinosa ((L.). The data offer the means for 3D space analysis of species distribution and stand structure around the circumboreal region. Furthermore, it can be used as a training data set for artificial intelligence (AI) applications and thereby improve our understanding of the boreal forest’s vegetation reorganization in response to significant global warming.

items.title: Branding in Migrant Entrepreneurship in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This chapter examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the branding processes of migrant entrepreneurs within the context of market integration and “mixed embeddedness.” The study evaluates how generative technologies facilitate the democratization of branding in small-scale entrepreneurship, help overcome cultural barriers, foster the development of dynamic capabilities, and mitigate the “liability of foreignness.” The work is based on theoretical analysis and a synthesis of existing empirical research. It analyzes both the strategic advantages of AI tools and the associated risks, such as visual homogenization, excessive content standardization, and a potential decline in consumer trust. Particular attention is paid to the migrant entrepreneurship ecosystem in Georgia, highlighting the significant role of digital technologies in the socio-economic integration of founders and the achievement of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

items.title: Capability, opportunity and motivation in university students’ generative AI usage
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in university learning, but academic engagement requires more than access or perceived usefulness. Drawing on the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation-Behaviour (COM-B) framework, this study examines associations between students’ capability, opportunity, motivation, and GenAI usage behaviour. The analysis uses cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from 533 students at four Ghanaian public universities and applies partial least squares structural equation modelling. Our results show that capability, opportunity, and motivation are positively associated with GenAI usage behaviour. Capability and opportunity are also positively associated with motivation and indirectly associated with GenAI usage behaviour through motivation. The model explains 28.1% of the variance in motivation and 35.2% of the variance in GenAI usage behaviour. These findings highlight the need for universities to integrate AI literacy, reliable infrastructure, lecturer guidance, clear institutional policies, and cultures supporting responsible academic use.
